scenes.headline: PyArrow & Columnar Data
scenes.subtitle: Fast Parquet with the Apache Arrow format
scenes.narration: PyArrow brings a fast, columnar, zero-copy data format to Python, and it is the engine that powers efficient reading and writing of the Parquet files at the heart of modern analytics.

scenes.headline: Row-oriented vs Columnar

columns.title: Columnar (Parquet)
points: Reads only the columns you need

scenes.narration: Row-oriented formats like CSV store each record's fields together, so scanning one column still forces you to read all of them. Columnar formats like Parquet store each column contiguously, which lets a query touch only the columns it needs and lets similar values compress tightly together. For analytical workloads that aggregate a few columns over billions of rows, columnar storage is dramatically faster and smaller.

scenes.headline: Why PyArrow matters
items: Arrow is a language-agnostic in-memory columnar standard
Zero-copy sharing with pandas, Polars, and DuckDB
Backs Parquet on disk and Flight for network transport
scenes.narration: Apache Arrow defines a single in-memory columnar layout that every tool can agree on, so data moves between pandas, Polars, and DuckDB without ever being serialized or copied. That shared representation is what makes cross-library workflows fast. The same format also underpins Parquet files on disk and the Flight protocol for shipping data across the network.

scenes.headline: Writing and reading Parquet
scenes.code:
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

table = pa.table({
    "id": [1, 2, 3],
    "amount": [9.5, 4.0, 7.25],
})

pq.write_table(table, "sales.parquet", compression="snappy")

back = pq.read_table("sales.parquet", columns=["amount"])
print(back.num_rows)
scenes.narration: Building an Arrow table from a dictionary of columns takes a single call, and write_table serializes it to Parquet with Snappy compression. On the way back in, the columns argument tells the reader to load only the amount column, skipping the id data entirely on disk. That column projection is the first and simplest way PyArrow saves you time and bytes.

scenes.headline: Predicate pushdown & row groups
scenes.code:
import pyarrow.dataset as ds

dataset = ds.dataset("sales/", format="parquet", partitioning="hive")

filtered = dataset.to_table(
    columns=["id", "amount"],
    filter=(ds.field("amount") > 5.0),
)
print(filtered.num_rows)
scenes.narration: The dataset API treats a whole directory of Parquet files as one logical table, understanding Hive-style partition folders automatically. When you pass a filter, PyArrow pushes that predicate down to the files, using row-group statistics to skip entire blocks whose values cannot match. Combined with column selection, this means a well-partitioned dataset can answer a query by reading only a tiny fraction of the bytes on disk.

scenes.headline: Typical DE flow
scenes.narration: A common pattern is to pay the conversion cost exactly once: ingest messy CSV or JSON, load it into an Arrow table, and write it out as partitioned Parquet. From then on, every downstream query benefits from column projection and predicate pushdown. You clean the data one time and reap fast, selective reads indefinitely.

scenes.headline: Best practices
items: Pick compression by goal: snappy for speed, zstd for smaller files
Partition on low-cardinality columns you filter on often
Right-size row groups, with 128 MB a common target
scenes.narration: Choose your compression codec by what you optimize for, using Snappy when read speed matters and Zstandard when storage cost dominates. Partition on columns you frequently filter by, but keep their cardinality low so you avoid a flood of tiny files. Finally, aim for row groups around 128 megabytes, which balances the granularity of pushdown against per-group overhead.

scenes.text: Columnar Parquet plus pushdown means you read only the bytes you actually need, not the whole file.
scenes.narration: PyArrow and Parquet transform analytical scans from brute-force full-file reads into surgical, compressed, column-level access. Master column projection and predicate pushdown and your queries will read only what they truly need.
